Problem: We want to understand why some college students choose not to attend professor office hours.
Rationale: This asks why students make a choice, which is about reasons and feelings, so Qualitative Research fits best. Exploratory Research or Field Research could also help uncover possible reasons.

Problem: Our company wants to know what percentage of customers prefer online shopping over shopping in person.
Rationale: The client wants a percentage, which means counting answers from many customers, so Quantitative Research fits best. Market Research also works because it's about customer preferences.

Problem: We want to determine whether a new tutoring program improves students' exam scores compared with students who do not use it.
Rationale: Comparing students who use the program with students who don't, to see if the program causes better scores, is what a Randomized Controlled Trial is for. Applied and Quantitative Research also fit because the goal is a practical, measurable result.

Problem: We want to understand how people's attitudes toward remote work change over a five-year period.
Rationale: The key phrase is 'over a five-year period'. Tracking how the same people change over time is Longitudinal Research. Quantitative or Qualitative Research could measure attitudes, but not the change over time as well.

Problem: Our city is considering a ban on single-use plastic bags. We want to understand how similar policies have affected waste in other cities.
Rationale: The city is deciding on a law and wants to know how similar laws worked elsewhere, which is Policy Research. A Systematic Review of past studies or Applied Research could also help.

Problem: We want to learn what teenagers think makes a social media app enjoyable to use.
Rationale: 'What teenagers think' is about opinions and experiences in their own words, so Qualitative Research fits best. Market Research or Exploratory Research could also help.

Problem: We have developed a prototype water bottle and want to test different lid designs to determine which is easiest to use.
Rationale: Testing prototype designs to make a product better is Product R&D. Applied or Quantitative Research could also be used to compare the lids.

Problem: Scientists want to better understand how a newly discovered protein interacts with human cells without developing an immediate commercial application.
Rationale: The scientists want to understand how something works, with no product in mind, which is Basic Research. Exploratory Research also fits because the protein is new.

Problem: We want to observe how customers actually move through our grocery store and which displays they stop at.
Rationale: The client wants to see what customers actually do in the real store, so researchers should watch on site, which is Field Research. Market Research or Qualitative Research could also help.

Problem: We want to determine whether students who sleep at least eight hours tend to have higher GPAs.
Rationale: Sleep hours and GPA are both numbers, and the question is whether they are related, so Quantitative Research fits best. Longitudinal Research could also follow students over time.

Problem: Our hospital wants to combine patient surveys with interviews to understand why patients miss scheduled appointments.
Rationale: The client wants to combine surveys (numbers) with interviews (experiences), which is Mixed Methods. Qualitative or Quantitative Research alone would only cover half of the question.

Problem: We want to combine the results of existing published studies to determine whether meditation reduces stress.
Rationale: Combining the results of studies that already exist is a Systematic Review. Quantitative Research also fits because the results are combined as numbers.

Problem: We don't know why users are abandoning our mobile application during account creation and want to investigate possible reasons.
Rationale: The client doesn't know why users leave yet and wants possible reasons, which is what Exploratory Research is for. Qualitative Research or Product R&D could also help find the problem.

Problem: A school wants to determine whether providing free breakfast improves student attendance.
Rationale: The school wants to solve a real, practical problem, so Applied Research fits best. Quantitative Research or a Randomized Controlled Trial could also measure whether attendance goes up.

Problem: Our company wants to know whether customers would be interested in buying a cheaper version of our current product.
Rationale: This is about whether customers would buy a product, which is Market Research. Quantitative or Qualitative Research could also be used to ask customers.

Problem: We want to interview first-generation college students about the challenges they experience during their first semester.
Rationale: Interviewing students about their challenges collects experiences in their own words, so Qualitative Research fits best. Exploratory or Field Research could also help.

Problem: We want to track the same group of graduates for ten years to see how their careers develop.
Rationale: Following the same group of graduates for ten years is exactly what Longitudinal Research does. Quantitative or Qualitative Research could be used along the way.

Problem: A state recently changed its minimum wage. We want to examine how the change affected employment and local businesses.
Rationale: The question is how a government policy change affected people and businesses, which is Policy Research. Quantitative or Applied Research could also measure the effects.

Problem: We want to test whether changing the color of a website's checkout button increases the percentage of visitors who complete a purchase.
Rationale: Showing visitors different button colors at random and comparing purchases is a Randomized Controlled Trial. Quantitative or Market Research also fit because it's about measuring what customers do.

Problem: Engineers want to investigate the fundamental properties of a new material before deciding what products it might be useful for.
Rationale: The engineers want to understand the material itself before thinking about uses, which is Basic Research. Exploratory Research also fits because the material is new.

Problem: We want researchers to spend time inside several classrooms observing how teachers and students use tablets during normal lessons.
Rationale: Researchers spending time in real classrooms during normal lessons is Field Research. Qualitative or Exploratory Research could also help.

Problem: We want to measure customer satisfaction numerically using a survey sent to 5,000 customers.
Rationale: Measuring satisfaction with numbers from 5,000 survey answers is Quantitative Research. Market Research also fits because it's about customers.

Problem: We want to understand both how many students use campus mental-health resources and what experiences students have when using them.
Rationale: The client wants both how many students use the resources (numbers) and what their experiences are (stories), which is Mixed Methods. Quantitative or Qualitative Research alone would only answer one part.

Problem: We are designing a new mobile application and want to repeatedly build and test prototypes with potential users.
Rationale: Building and testing prototypes with users again and again is Product R&D. Applied or Qualitative Research could also help.

Problem: We want to examine all high-quality published research comparing remote learning with classroom learning.
Rationale: Looking at all the high-quality published research on one question is a Systematic Review. Quantitative Research also fits if the results are combined as numbers.

Problem: A restaurant wants to understand which new menu items its target customers would be most likely to purchase.
Rationale: Finding out what target customers would most likely buy is Market Research. Quantitative or Qualitative Research could also be used to ask them.

Problem: We have noticed employees leaving our company more frequently, but we don't know why and want to identify possible explanations.
Rationale: The company has noticed a problem but doesn't know why, so the first step is Exploratory Research to find possible explanations. Qualitative Research or Mixed Methods could also help.

Problem: A factory wants to determine whether a new workflow can reduce the average time required to assemble a product.
Rationale: The factory wants to solve a practical problem, assembly time, so Applied Research fits best. Quantitative Research or a Randomized Controlled Trial could also measure the change.

Problem: We want to study how residents actually use a newly constructed public park during different times of day.
Rationale: Studying how people actually use the park at different times means watching on site, which is Field Research. Qualitative or Quantitative Research could also help.

Problem: We want to follow children from elementary school through high school to study how reading habits develop as they age.
Rationale: Following the same children from elementary school through high school is Longitudinal Research. Quantitative or Qualitative Research could be used along the way.

Problem: The university is considering changing its parking rules. We want to investigate how the proposed policy could affect students and employees.
Rationale: The university is weighing a rule change and wants to know how it could affect people, which is Policy Research. Mixed Methods or Applied Research could also help.

Problem: We want to collect numerical pollution measurements and interview residents to understand both pollution levels and how residents believe pollution affects their neighborhood.
Rationale: Pollution measurements (numbers) plus interviews with residents (experiences) is Mixed Methods. Quantitative or Qualitative Research alone would only cover one part.

Problem: We want to determine whether people assigned to use a new study technique perform better on a memory test than people assigned to use their normal technique.
Rationale: People are assigned to either the new technique or their normal one and then compared on a test, which is a Randomized Controlled Trial. Quantitative or Applied Research also fit.

Problem: Our engineering team wants to create and test several versions of a low-cost air-quality sensor before choosing a final design.
Rationale: Building and testing several versions of the sensor before picking a final design is Product R&D. Applied or Quantitative Research could also help.

Problem: Which video game is objectively the greatest video game ever made?
Rationale: 'The greatest video game ever' is a matter of opinion, so no evidence could prove an objective answer. This one can't be researched.

Problem: We need researchers to prove that our company's product is better than every competitor's product, regardless of what the evidence shows.
Rationale: Research has to follow the evidence. A study that must reach a set answer 'regardless of what the evidence shows' isn't research.

Problem: Can you tell us exactly what the stock market will be worth twenty years from today?
Rationale: No study can tell the exact future value of the stock market. Research can look at trends, but it can't give an exact answer twenty years out.

Problem: We want a study proving that our CEO is the best CEO in the country, regardless of what the evidence shows.
Rationale: 'The best CEO' depends on opinion, and the client wants a set answer regardless of the evidence. That isn't something research can do.

Problem: Can researchers determine whether pineapple belongs on pizza once and for all?
Rationale: Whether pineapple belongs on pizza is personal taste. Research could measure how many people like it, but it can't settle whether it 'belongs'.

Problem: We want to know the exact thoughts every American will have about artificial intelligence ten years from now.
Rationale: No one can know the exact thoughts of every American ten years from now. Research can study opinions today, but it can't predict exact future thoughts.
